First, niacin, 32 milligrams is niacinamide. Also known as vitamin B3 plays a key role in energy production, the maintenance of healthy skin, nervous system function and DNA synthesis. Niacin supplementation has been associated with improved sensory register, which is the short-term storage of memory received through the environment and short-term memory. The literature available suggests this is facilitated through enhanced neuronal transmission. Next up, P5P, vitamin B6, methylated B6, as pyridoxal-5-phosphate, 20 milligrams. So much like other B vitamins, B6 plays several overlapping roles in supporting optimal function, but with that said, the main attribute of interest in this formula is the impact it has on the production of neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine, also known as noreadrenaline. L-dopa, levodopa, is the precursor to dopamine, meaning that it is converted into dopamine in the brain and this conversion process is facilitated by an enzyme called aromatic amino acid D carboxylase, L-dopa D carboxylase, which requires P5P, methylated B6, as a cofactor. So I chose to include activated B6, P5P instead of the commonly used pyridoxine HCl because the conversion process directly requires P5P. In addition, literature shows that supplementing with inactive B6, pyridoxine, may competitively inhibit activated B6 from working and could even paradoxically lead to a B6 deficiency through the supplementation of pyridoxine HCl. So adequate B6 status is critical for downstream dopaminergic neurotransmission and is why we included the P5P. B12 as methylcobalamin, 250 micrograms. B12 is required for the development, myelination and function of the central nervous system. Contextually in this formula, B12 acts as a cofactor in the synthesis of neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine and deficiency in B12 can lead to decreased production of neurotransmitters, effect cognitive function and cause symptoms such as fatigue and lethargy. Cyanocobalamin and methylcobalamin are probably the most common two forms of B12. Methylcobalamin is the biologically active form and cyanocobalamin is the most common form found in supplements and fortified foods. I included methylcobalamin specifically because it is a better methyl donor compared to cyanocobalamin and some studies have suggested that methylcobalamin supplementation may have a positive impact on neurotransmitter function and ultimately just having activated B vitamins I feel like is probably a better move. What is the optimal creatine dose that should everyone use five grams per day? In most studies, a loading protocol of around 0.3 grams per kilogram of body weight per day was utilized for five to seven days, followed by a daily maintenance dose of at least 0.03 grams per kilogram of body weight. So for an 180-pound person, 82 kilograms, this equates to a loading phase dosage of 25 grams per day and a maintenance dose of at least 2.5 grams per day thereafter. Alternatively, taking a three to five gram dose of creatine per day without a loading phase will still reach the same net outcome in most individuals. It just takes a bit longer to reach saturation, and this is where the five gram per day dosage most of us have been told to follow derived from. What most don't know though, is that larger athletes engaged in intense training may need to consume five to 10 grams per day of creatine to maintain optimal or capacity whole body creatine stores and clinical populations may need to consume 10 to 30 grams per day throughout their lifespan to offset creatine synthesis deficiencies and or provide therapeutic benefit in various disease states. Even long-term, high dose ingestion of creatine up to 30 grams per day for up to five years and patient populations has not been associated with an increased incidence of renal dysfunction. So getting into the effects on muscular strength, power, and size of betaine supplementation first off. A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial examined the ergogenic effects of betaine supplementation, 1.25 grams taken twice per day on strength and power performance in an array of high intensity strength slash power resistance exercises including bench press, squat, and jump tests. Subjects were matched accordingly to age, body size, and training experience before their random placements into either the betaine supplementation or placebo groups for 14 days. Total attention was given to dietary and activity control among and within subjects. Subjects submitted 3-day diet records and 6-week activity reports and all subjects reported similar physical activity and diet before each exercise, test, and throughout study participation. A standardized whole body resistance training session was performed twice during the supplementation periods to maintain the subjects' level of conditioning and subjects were instructed to refrain from any exercise for 48 hours before the performance testing sessions. After 14 days in the betaine group, isometric bench press force increased up to 24.61%, isometric bench press throw power increased up to 15.97%, isometric squat force increased up to 21.43%, and vertical jump power increased up to 14.22%. The placebo group had no improvement in those performance metrics. Another randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial examined the effect of betaine supplementation, 1.25 grams taken twice per day on cycling sprint performance. Subjects included resistance-trained men and women who are matched paired based on baseline maximum peak power and assigned to either betaine or placebo group for 7 days. There was no training involved during the supplementation period. The initial supplementation period was followed by a 3-week washout phase and then subjects were assigned to the opposite group for another 7 days. The maximum peak power during a cycling sprint test was increased by 5.75% after supplementation with betaine with no difference in power in the placebo group from baseline. Another study investigated the effects of long-term betaine supplementation, 1.25 grams twice per day on body composition, performance and homocysteine, thylactone in experienced strength-trained men. Subjects were tested prior to and following 6 weeks of treatment. Arm and thigh cross-sectional area was estimated via girth and skin-fold measurements. Bone density was estimated via skin-fold calipers and used to estimate body fat percentage, fat mass and lean body mass. This was assessed via vertical jump, bench press 1 rep max and back squat 1 rep max. Arm size significantly increased in the betaine group but not placebo group. Bench press training volume was significantly improved in the betaine group compared to the placebo group at micro cycles 1 and 3. Body fat percentage, fat mass and lean body mass improved significantly in the betaine group but not in the placebo group. No differences were found in performance variables between groups except that it was a trend for increased vertical jump power in the betaine group versus the placebo group. A significant interaction existed for homocysteine thylactone with increases from baseline to week 2 in the placebo group but not in the betaine group. Additionally, homocysteine thylactone remained elevated at week 4 in the placebo group but not in the betaine group. It is speculated that these results are achieved primarily through the osmolytic effects of betaine and its attenuation of lactate increases during exercise. Moving on to the next ingredient in the formula, 400 milligrams caffeine and hydrous. Caffeine is the most well known central nervous system stimulant on earth. It is well known for potent effects on wakefulness, alertness, attentional performance and power output. When a person is awake and alert, little adenosine is present in CNS neurons. Throughout the day, adenosine accumulates in the neuronal synapse binding to and activating adenosine receptors found on certain CNS neurons. The activation of these adenosine receptors increases sleepiness. When caffeine is consumed, it binds to and antagonizes adenosine receptors preventing adenosine from binding to and activating the receptor. As a result, caffeine temporarily prevents or relieves drowsiness and thus maintains or restores alertness. What is the minimum effective dose of caffeine? The minimum effective dose of caffeine varies depending on several factors, including an individual's body weight, tolerance to caffeine, and sensitivity to its effects. Research suggests that the minimum effective dose of caffeine is likely around 40 to 50 milligrams, which is roughly equivalent to a small cup of coffee. However, other studies assessing just how low of a dose can yield positive effects have found that surprisingly low dosages still move the needle. A double blind study measured the effects of 0, 12.5, 25, 50, and 100 milligrams of caffeine on cognitive performance, mood, and thirst in adults with low and moderate to high habitual caffeine intakes. 12.5 milligrams caffeine improved cognitive performance during both simple and stressful demanding tasks. This amount of caffeine is equivalent to about a quarter of a serving of tea and less than a quarter of a serving of coffee. On a body weight basis, 12.5 milligrams equated to 0.18 milligrams per kilogram. At the time, that was reported to be the lowest dose of caffeine to reliably affect cognitive performance in human adults. So that begs the question, what is the caffeine dose necessary for enhanced mental or physical performance? Following low, approximately 40 milligrams or 0.5 milligrams per kilogram, to moderate, 300 milligrams approximately, or 4 milligrams per kilogram, caffeine doses, alertness, vigilance, attention, and reaction time improve. However, less consistent effects are observed on memory and higher order executive functions such as judgment and decision making. In terms of physical performance, the minimum effective dose of caffeine for improving metrics such as time to exhaustion, muscle strength, endurance, and high intensity sprints has been shown to be about 3 to 6 milligrams per kilogram of body weight or roughly 200 to 400 milligrams for a 150 pound, 68 kilogram person. Very high doses of caffeine, for example, 9 milligrams per kilogram are associated with a high incidence of side effects and do not seem to be required to elicit an organic effect. All that said, it's worth noting that some people may experience both cognitive and physical performance benefits at much lower dosages while others may need a much higher dosage to see an effect. Normally, healthy adults can safely consume up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day. However, that doesn't mean that you need to use that high of a dose. Our stim-free formula with our Swiss Army knife stacked with new tropics and stims formula. Should you wait 90 minutes after waking up to take caffeine? Interesting question and something many people have started to implement and encourage as well is delaying the intake of caffeine for 90 to 120 minutes after waking up. The logic behind this approach is to prevent an afternoon crash that purportedly occurs of caffeine is taken upon waking. This is hinged on the relationship between adenosine and cortisol and the purported natural clearance of adenosine that is incomplete upon waking, which isn't actually the case, but it is also said that adenosine flooding the receptors will be more likely to cause a sleepiness rebound effect and the crash, if you call it. If you ingest caffeine shortly after waking up, whereas you can avoid that adenosine rebound by delaying caffeine intake for one and a half to two hours. I feel like it's worthwhile to talk about the adenosine and cortisol diurnal rhythm and just understand how they work. To evaluate the validity of this theory, should we delay our intake, it's best to evaluate really what these levels look like on a 24-hour basis of cortisol and adenosine, of the average healthy person. Adenosine levels are highest when you go to sleep and as you sleep, adenosine levels start to decrease and cortisol levels bottom out during the first half of the night. In the latter half, cortisol levels start to ramp up and adenosine levels are at the lowest point of the day right before you wake up and they start immediately increasing again after waking, subsequently building up sleep pressure over the course of the day and cortisol levels peak shortly after you wake up. In healthy individuals, there is typically a spike in and peaking in cortisol levels within 15 to 45 minutes of waking up. This increase in cortisol signals the body to mobilize and get going and cortisol then declines steadily over the day thereafter while adenosine has already been increasing since waking up and the cycle repeats itself on a 24-hour basis. When caffeine is consumed, it binds to and antagonizes adenosine receptors preventing adenosine from binding to whatever capacity relative to your dose, adenosine receptor density, etc., myriad of factors but ultimately that's the mechanism. This action temporarily inhibits drowsiness and helps maintain or restore alertness. As caffeine use increases both adrenocortico-tropin, ECTH and cortisol secretion, it has been speculated that delaying caffeine ingestion until 90 to 120 minutes after waking will allow an individual to take advantage of their natural endogenous cortisol spike in the morning and then cruise through the afternoon without any crash that could otherwise be caused by a flooding of the adenosine receptors as caffeine is eliminated. No literature exists that I'm aware of supporting that an afternoon crash is an expected outcome after caffeine intake. It doesn't mean we should disregard it though, especially if many people have noted this now anecdotally, but the first consideration I would make regarding this theory is that over time with regular use, which is how most people use caffeine, the caffeine-mediated cortisol spike appears to be blunted or eliminated entirely. In addition, adenosine is not decreasing more over those 90 minutes. On the contrary, adenosine is lowest when you wake up. It increases thereafter building up sleep pressure over the day, but there is no adenosine clearance occurring after waking where it's still working its way to your system as cortisol is going up. Adenosine is at its lowest and now the sleep pressure begins to rise upon waking. Typically caffeine is taken to achieve a higher level of cognitive function, vigilance, sports performance or general wakefulness. For most daily users, I speculate that delaying caffeine intake for one and a half to two hours is probably just delaying you getting the effects you want and making it more likely to impede your sleep quality later. Even if this afternoon crash existed, the total daily caffeine dosage could also be split up to allow for redosing. I speculate that most, but maybe not all, but most afternoon caffeine crashes are driven primarily through individual specific lifestyle, sleep hygiene, diet, exercise or caffeine dose and duration of exposure and are kind of like minimally influenced by adenosine flooding the receptors just hours after caffeine ingestion. Moving on to the next ingredient, synactive. This is a very popular one or at least it seemingly is. Synescent cells are cells that have permanently stopped dividing but do not undergo cell death. They are in a state of permanent growth arrest but remain metabolically active, often secreting inflammatory cytokines, growth factors and proteases. Synescent cells accumulate with age and contribute to the aging process by promoting inflammation and tissue dysfunction. Their presence is associated with age-related conditions such as arthritis, cardiovascular disease and neurodegenerative diseases. Sennilitics are drugs or compounds that can selectively induce death of these senescent cells and potentially reducing as a result of that age-related tissue damage and improving overall health span. Synactive is a branded compound or I should say blend, proprietary blend that is marketed as one of these sennilitics primarily for athletic performance. It's a prop blend of two plant extracts, Panax, Nodo ginseng and Rosa Roxbury.
